meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The lion who breaks the enemy's ranks is a minor hero compared to the lion who overcomes himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Rumi, modern English. The verse is Masnavi I, 1389; the polished wording people share is a 1990 rendering, not a literal translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1207–1273 · Persian poet, Islamic scholar and Sufi mystic
answer.sourceLine: This one is real. The thought is Rumi’s own — Masnavi, Book I, verse 1389, sitting inside the passage on the ‘greater jihád,’ the war against the self. What is not thirteenth-century is the English: the polished one-liner people share is a modern rendering credited to Camille Adams Helminski and Kabir Helminski, whereas a literal translation of the same couplet reads “Deem of small account the lion (champion) who breaks the ranks (of the enemy): the (true) lion is he that breaks (conquers) himself.”

source.heading: Where the line actually sits

docMeta.dd: Book I, verse 1389 — the ‘greater jihád’ passage, opening the story of ‘Umar and the ambassador of Rúm
Dictated over roughly twelve years in Anatolia; left unfinished at Rumi’s death in 1273
Popular wording: modern English rendering commonly credited to Camille Adams Helminski and Kabir Helminski (1990). Literal English of Books I–II: Reynold A. Nicholson, Luzac & Co., 1926.

source.excerpt: When I turned back from the outer warfare, I set my face towards the inner warfare. We have returned from the lesser Jihád, we are engaged along with the Prophet in the greater Jihád… Deem of small account the lion (champion) who breaks the ranks (of the enemy): the (true) lion is he that breaks (conquers) himself.
trail: Wikiquote’s Rumi page ↗ carries the exact popular wording in its Masnavi section with the citation “I, 1389” — and, unusually for that section, no translator credit, which is the first hint that the English is someone’s rendering rather than a standard edition.

Checking that verse number independently: masnavi.net’s Book I, verse 1389 ↗ gives the Persian couplet with a literal English rendering — “Deem of small account the lion (champion) who breaks the ranks (of the enemy): the (true) lion is he that breaks (conquers) himself” — confirming the verse says exactly this, at exactly that number.

The preceding verses, 1385–1392 ↗, place it: the turn from “the lesser Jihád” to “the greater Jihád,” then the arrival of the Byzantine emperor’s ambassador at Medina. So the line is structural, not a detached aphorism.

For the standard scholarly English, the title page of the Internet Archive’s scan of Nicholson’s volume ↗ confirms it as Reynold A. Nicholson’s translation of the First and Second Books, printed by Cambridge University Press for the Trustees of the E. J. W. Gibb Memorial and published by Luzac & Co., London, 1926.
source.excerptNote: The literal English rendering shown at masnavi.net for Book I ↗, where the bracketed words are the translator’s clarifications. The familiar one-line version is a smoothed modern rendering of the final couplet.

source.rightsNote: Two separate clocks run here. Rumi’s thirteenth-century Persian is long in the public domain, and Reynold A. Nicholson’s literal English translation of Books I and II — published in 1926 — is public domain in the United States. But the exact wording in circulation is a modern rendering commonly credited to Camille Adams Helminski and Kabir Helminski in 1990, and a 1990 translation is a copyrightable work in its own right. Treat the polished one-liner as in copyright and credit the translators; the 1926 literal rendering is the freely reusable text.

author.name: Rumi
author.heading: Who Rumi actually was
author.metaLine: 1207–1273 · Persian poet, Islamic scholar and Sufi mystic
author.bio: Jalāl al-Dīn Muḥammad Rūmī was born in 1207 in Wakhsh, in what is now Tajikistan, and settled as a young man in Konya in Anatolia, where he taught, preached and eventually founded the order remembered in the West as the whirling dervishes. He was a working Islamic scholar and jurist long before he was a poet; the poetry came late, after his encounter with the wandering mystic Shams of Tabriz. His masterwork, the six-book Masnavi — some 27,000 lines dictated over roughly twelve years and left unfinished at his death in 1273 — is so revered in Persian that it has been called “the Qur’an in Persian.”

cite.sourceCitation: Jalāl al-Dīn Rūmī, Masnaví, Book I, verse 1389. English translation of Books I–II: Reynold A. Nicholson, The Mathnawí of Jalálu’ddín Rúmí, vol. 2 (London: Luzac & Co., 1926). The widely shared modern English wording is commonly credited to Rumi Daylight: A Daybook of Spiritual Guidance, trans. Camille Adams Helminski and Kabir Helminski (1990).

misattribution.heading: Right author, borrowed voice
misattribution.intro: Rumi is one of the internet’s biggest magnets for invented quotations, so the useful question here is not “is it his?” — it is — but “whose English is it?”

items.who: Camille Adams Helminski and Kabir Helminski
items.why: The fluent one-liner is twentieth-century English. Quote databases that bother to cite anything credit it to Rumi Daylight: A Daybook of Spiritual Guidance (1990) ↗, and the exact sentence appears among Rumi verses selected by Kabir Helminski on his own organisation’s site ↗. A literal translation of the couplet reads quite differently.

Shared alone it reads as generic self-improvement. In the poem it is the closing beat of an argument about the greater struggle against the self, and it hands straight off to the story of the Byzantine ambassador who cannot find the Caliph’s palace — visible in verses 1385–1392 ↗.

Much of the Rumi circulating in English is re-written rather than translated — a problem documented at length in Dar al-Masnavi’s critique of popular versions ↗. This line is a comparatively faithful case, but the habit of quoting Rumi with no book or verse number is why so many fakes survive.

misattribution.truthLine: Verdict: the thought and the verse are genuinely Rumi’s — Wikiquote pins the wording to Masnavi I, 1389 ↗ — but the sentence you are sharing is modern English, and deserves to be credited as a rendering.

context.heading: The war you don’t get a medal for
lead: The couplet does not arrive as a standalone aphorism. It closes a short, fierce run of verses in which the speaker turns from external battle to internal battle: “When I turned back from the outer warfare, I set my face towards the inner warfare… We have returned from the lesser Jihád, we are engaged along with the Prophet in the greater Jihád.” Rumi is invoking a distinction well known in Islamic tradition — the lesser struggle is the one fought with armies, the greater one is fought against the nafs, the appetitive self.

Then, having set that up, the lion line lands as the punchline — and immediately Rumi cuts to a story that dramatises it: an ambassador from the Byzantine emperor arrives in Medina looking for the Caliph’s palace, and is told “He has no palace: ‘Umar’s (only) palace is an illumined spirit.” The battlefield hero and the imperial envoy are both measuring the wrong thing.
detailsBody: Reynold A. Nicholson’s Cambridge-printed edition, issued for the Trustees of the E. J. W. Gibb Memorial, was the first complete English Masnavi; the volume carrying Books I and II in English appeared in 1926. Nicholson’s method was deliberately unlovely — he bracketed his own clarifying words in parentheses so a reader could see exactly where the Persian stopped and the translator started. That is why the literal line bristles with “(champion)” and “(conquers).”

The versions that circulate online do the opposite: they smooth the parentheses away. That is a legitimate thing to do with poetry, and the Helminski rendering is a faithful reading of the sense. It just means the sentence being shared is a twentieth-century English sentence, and should be cited as one.
